notable_claims: The Ohio State ACS policy lacks due process protections for users who are denied access to computer systems.
University policies should be developed with the broadest possible participation of the academic community.
Requiring users to sign agreements that potentially impinge on First, Fifth, and 14th Amendment rights may be legally untenable.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie provides a detailed critique of the Office of Academic Computing's (ACS) computer use policy at The Ohio State University. He argues that the policy is overly vague, lacks guarantees for privacy and freedom of expression, and fails to provide due process protections for users facing expulsion from the system. Kadie contrasts the ACS policy with the 'Joint Statement on Rights and Freedoms of Students' to highlight the absence of procedural safeguards.
classification.title: Re: Ohio State ACS policy

notable_claims: User acknowledgment forms do not make unreasonable searches of computer files legal.
University policies prohibiting 'offensive' or 'demeaning' electronic speech may violate the US Constitution and academic freedom.
Computer expulsion procedures should include detailed due process, including appeal mechanisms and formal hearings.
organizations: University of Texas Dept. of CS
classification.summary: Carl Kadie provides a legal critique of the University of Texas Computer Science Department's use policy, arguing that its terms regarding file searches and speech restrictions are overly broad. He contends that computer files should receive protections similar to physical office spaces and that restricting 'offensive' speech likely violates the First Amendment. The post includes an extensive bibliography of case law and legal guides relevant to academic freedom and electronic communication.
classification.title: Re: Computer Use Policy of U. Texas Dept. of CS

identity.subject: Re: Computer Use Policy of U. Texas Dept. of CS

notable_claims: The Owlnet agreement allows system management to examine all data and files without prior consent.
There is a potential conflict between digital user agreements and university-wide privacy policies regarding student possessions.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie critiques the user agreement for Rice University's Owlnet system, specifically questioning a clause that allows system management to examine any data without consent. He compares this digital policy to physical privacy protections and student rights regarding searches of personal possessions.
classification.title: Re: Rice University's Owlnet User Agreement

identity.subject: Re: Rice University's Owlnet User Agreement

notable_claims: Disciplinary procedures were being informed by the draft Statement on Computers and Academic Freedom.
Immediate lockout is used for system security or integrity incidents to prevent damage and force a meeting with administration.
Users have the right to a fair hearing by the Owlnet Steering Committee for violations not referred to external authorities.
classification.summary: Joseph A. Watters publishes the disciplinary and due process procedures for Rice University's Owlnet computing system. The document outlines a tiered system of punishments ranging from warnings to permanent access revocation and describes the appeal process via the student handbook. Notably, the author mentions that these procedures were being refined based on student input and the draft Statement on Computers and Academic Freedom.
classification.title: Rice Univ, Owlnet Disciplinary Procedures

notable_claims: Computing policies at Rice required prior permission for offsite email or FTP.
Users faced account lockouts without warning as a penalty for mistakes.
The administrative atmosphere was described as bureaucratic, coldly legal, and oppressive to creativity.
classification.summary: A student at Rice University discusses the oppressive nature of the Owlnet computing policies. The post highlights a culture of bureaucratic control where creativity and exploration are discouraged by the threat of account lockouts. It describes the university's Information Systems (IS) department as acting like 'police' over undergraduate engineering networks.
classification.title: Re: Rice University's Owlnet and University Computing Policies

identity.subject: [comp.admin.policy]  Re: Rice University's Owlnet and University Computing Policies

notable_claims: Some Rice University students viewed administrative open meetings as misdirection following protests.
Access denials on Owlnet occurred without prior warning even in cases not threatening system security.
classification.summary: Douglas Triggs discusses the application of computing policies at Rice University's Owlnet in response to a discussion about student expulsions. He disputes claims that users are always given warnings before access denial, noting his own experience with an immediate lockout. He also expresses skepticism regarding an upcoming open meeting intended to formulate internal Owlnet processes.

The author notes that a user was censored by their sysadmin following a controversial post.

notable_claims: The purpose of interlibrary loan is to obtain material for research and serious study not available locally.
Borrowing libraries are responsible for screening requests to ensure they conform to established codes.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie explores the analogy between NSFnet and interlibrary loan systems to determine appropriate acceptable use policies. He references the National Interlibrary Loan Code (1980) and a model code from the American Library Association to compare standards for resource access and screening.
classification.title: interlibrary loan policy

notable_claims: The responsibility for following NSFnet rules should fall on the person requesting a transfer, not the archive owner.
Restricting non-academic material via FTP is analogous to an interlibrary system forbidding libraries from offering non-research materials.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie uses an analogy between the NSFnet and interlibrary loan systems to argue against restricting anonymous FTP access. He suggests that responsibility for adhering to network usage rules should lie with the requester rather than the archive owner. This argues against the National Science Foundation's ability to dictate what non-academic material can be hosted on servers connected to the network.
classification.title: Re: interlibrary loan policy

notable_claims: Student was dismissed for violations of the Code of Student Conduct including unauthorized use of Academic Computing Services facilities and equipment.
classification.summary: Steve Brack shared his official dismissal letter from The Ohio State University following a hearing by the University Judicial Panel. He was found guilty of unauthorized use of university property and services, specifically involving Academic Computing Services facilities. While cleared of dishonest conduct, he was dismissed for four quarters.
classification.title: Steve Brack's Letter of Dismissal

notable_claims: The university failed to provide the correspondence between alleged actions and specific rule violations.
The lack of clear charges constituted a violation of procedural due process guaranteed by the Constitution.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie critiques the dismissal of student Steve Brack from Ohio State University, arguing that the university failed to provide procedural due process. Kadie asserts that while Brack was given a list of alleged actions and rules, he was not informed of the specific charges or how his actions violated those rules.
classification.title: Re: Steve Brack's Letter of Dismissal

identity.subject: Re: Steve Brack's Letter of Dismissal

notable_claims: Ohio State's refusal to specify charges makes it impossible for Steven Brack to defend himself.
Due process requires that students be given specific, clear, and full reasons for proposed disciplinary action.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie argues that Ohio State University's refusal to provide Steven Brack with specific charges for his dismissal prevents a proper defense and likely violates the law. To support this, Kadie quotes legal texts regarding the right to adequate notice in student disciplinary proceedings. The text emphasizes that vague charges of 'misconduct' are insufficient for due process.
classification.title: Re: Steve Brack's Letter of Dismissal

identity.subject: Re: Steve Brack's Letter of Dismissal

notable_claims: ACS is not listed as an entity authorized to impose sanctions in the OSU handbook.
The action taken against Brack was framed as administrative rather than disciplinary to avoid due process requirements.
classification.summary: Steven Brack discusses his expulsion from computing services at Ohio State University (OSU). He argues that the Academic Computing Services (ACS) bypassed formal disciplinary procedures by framing their action as an administrative one, thereby avoiding due process and appeal mechanisms defined in the student handbook.
